node.label: Black Canadian history
node.period_rationale: The field became an academic literature in 'Reorientations, c. 1970–85': Winks (1971) and Walker's Black Loyalists (1976), with Walker's guide (1980), Hill (1981) and Walker's CHA publication (1985); Walker dates the Community orientation to this turn and the social-history movement. Trudel (1960) is earlier work. Growth continued in period_3 (Calliste 1987, Walker 1989, Brand 1991, We're Rooted Here 1994, Walker 1997, Cahill–Walker 1999), and most uptake is post-2000: of the 20 works most cited by 2009–2026 PhDs (first-publication years), 4 date from 1960–85, 7 from 1986–2000 and 9 after 2000 (median 1998). period_3 is a defensible alternative; the entry is placed where the field formed.
node.date_label: Earlier work: Trudel on slavery in French Canada 1960 · Winks's survey 1971 · Walker's Black Loyalists 1976 · Calliste on sleeping car porters 1987 · Brand's oral history of Black working women 1991 · We're Rooted Here, African Canadian women's history 1994 · Walker's five orientations 1997 · Cahill–Walker Black Loyalist exchange 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000, selected later works

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1960 (Trudel) is earlier work, not a field origin; Walker (1997) also names older writers (Landon, Riddell) whom he classes as the 'Clients' orientation. 1999 is the last selected in-period milestone; post-2000 work sits in extension_coverage.

node.description: Historical writing on people of African descent in Canada: slavery in New France and British North America, Black Loyalists and refugees, fugitive slaves and the settlements of Canada West, Black communities and churches, migration from the United States and the Caribbean, and racism in work, law and the state. Marcel Trudel documented slavery in French Canada (1960; dictionary 1990). After earlier work by Landon, Riddell and Trudel, Robin Winks's survey The Blacks in Canada (1971), which Walker reviewed critically, and James Walker's The Black Loyalists (1976), which put Black community at the centre; Winks credited it with ending the 'victims' school. From the late 1980s Agnes Calliste studied sleeping car porters and Caribbean migrants, Dorothy Williams Black Montreal, and Dionne Brand and the authors of We're Rooted Here (1994) Black women's history. In 1997 Walker sorted the historiography into five orientations by the role it gives Black people, from 'clients' of white philanthropy (Landon, Riddell) through 'victims' and 'achievers' to 'community' and 1990s 'survivors', and argued that community is the key. Barry Cahill called the Black Loyalists a scholars' myth that sidelined the enslaved (1999); Walker replied, placing his book in the civil-rights era. After 2000 the field grew around slavery (Cooper, Whitfield, Mackey), migration and labour (Mathieu), law (Barrington Walker) and Black Montreal (Austin, Mills), countering the image of Canada as a haven at the end of the Underground Railroad.
node.scope_note: A research field on people of African descent in Canada, defined by its subject, from slavery in New France to Black migration, community and racism. Created on the user's decision of 2026-10-12 (Q46): it was a strand of cdn_immigration_ethnicity, and Walker's 1997 essay treats it as its own historiography. Its relation to immigration history is a comparison, not a hierarchy; works on Black migration and immigration control (Calliste 1993–94, Shepard 1997) are cross-referenced in that entry. Several roster people have primary placements elsewhere (Trudel: quebec_historiography; Mills: cdn_sixties; Austin is also in cdn_sixties). Community and non-academic historians (Hill, Brand, Ruck, Mackey) are included because Walker's reading list and PhD bibliographies use them; Ruck and Forsythe are cited as community and participants' accounts. Indigenous slavery in New France (panis) is not covered; Rushforth's Bonds of Alliance (2012; 20 PhDs), whose title pairs Indigenous and Atlantic slaveries, is excluded from the counts because its Black-history content was not checked.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Trudel, L'esclavage au Canada français (1960). Winks, The Blacks in Canada (1971; 2nd ed. 1997); Walker, The Black Loyalists (1976), A History of Blacks in Canada (1980), Racial Discrimination in Canada (1985), "Race and Recruitment in World War I" (1989), "Allegories and Orientations in African-Canadian Historiography" (1997) and "Myth, History and Revisionism" (1999); Hill, The Freedom-Seekers (1981); Silverman, Unwelcome Guests (1985); Calliste, "Sleeping Car Porters in Canada" (1987) and "Race, Gender and Canadian Immigration Policy" (1993–94); Ruck, The Black Battalion (1987, community history); Williams, Blacks in Montreal (1989) and The Road to Now (1997); Trudel, Dictionnaire des esclaves (1990); Brand, No Burden to Carry (1991); Stouffer, The Light of Nature and the Law of God (1992); Bristow, Brand, Carty, Cooper, Hamilton and Shadd, We're Rooted Here (1994); Shepard, Deemed Unsuitable (1997); Clairmont and Magill, Africville (1974; 1987); Cahill, "The Black Loyalist Myth in Atlantic Canada" (1999). Contemporary: Forsythe, ed., Let the Niggers Burn! (1971). Extension: Gay, Les Noirs du Québec (2004); Cooper, The Hanging of Angélique (2006); Whitfield, Blacks on the Border (2006) and North to Bondage (2016); Austin, "All Roads Led to Montreal" (2007) and Fear of a Black Nation (2013); Nelson, Razing Africville (2008); Mackey, Done with Slavery (2010); Mathieu, North of the Color Line (2010); B. Walker, Race on Trial (2010); Flynn, Moving Beyond Borders (2011); Mills, A Place in the Sun (2016); Morton and Wright, "Black History in Atlantic Canada: A Bibliography" (2021).

representative_people.works: L'esclavage au Canada français (1960); Dictionnaire des esclaves et de leurs propriétaires au Canada français (1990); Deux siècles d'esclavage au Québec (2004, extension)

representative_people.name: Robin W. Winks
representative_people.context: An American historian's survey of Black Canadians, which Walker in 1997 still called the outstanding reference work; Walker reviewed it critically in 1971, and Winks credited The Black Loyalists with ending the 'victims' school.
representative_people.works: The Blacks in Canada: A History (1971; 2nd ed. 1997)

representative_people.name: James W. St. G. Walker
representative_people.context: Puts Black community at the centre of the Black Loyalist story (1976); writes the field's guide (1980), a CHA publication on discrimination (1985) and a study of race in First World War recruitment (1989); in 1997 maps five orientations in African-Canadian historiography and in 1999 answers Cahill.
representative_people.works: The Black Loyalists (1976); A History of Blacks in Canada (1980); Racial Discrimination in Canada (1985); "Race and Recruitment in World War I" (1989); "Allegories and Orientations" (1997); "Myth, History and Revisionism" (1999)

representative_people.name: Daniel G. Hill
representative_people.context: A sociologist and historian whose history of Black people in early Canada Walker recommended for introductory reading.
representative_people.works: The Freedom-Seekers: Blacks in Early Canada (1981)

representative_people.name: Agnes Calliste
representative_people.context: Studies Black sleeping car porters and the racialized control of Caribbean labour migration.
representative_people.works: "Sleeping Car Porters in Canada" (1987); "Race, Gender and Canadian Immigration Policy" (1993–94)

representative_people.name: Dionne Brand
representative_people.context: A poet and writer who edits interviews with Black working women in Ontario; Walker read her introduction as 'Survivors' and the interviews as 'Community'.
representative_people.works: No Burden to Carry (1991); co-author, We're Rooted Here (1994)

representative_people.name: Peggy Bristow
representative_people.context: First-named of six authors of the collective volume on African Canadian women's history.
representative_people.works: 'We're Rooted Here and They Can't Pull Us Up' (1994)

representative_people.name: Dorothy W. Williams
representative_people.context: Writes the long-run history of Black Montreal, from its demography (1989) to a narrative history (1997).
representative_people.works: Blacks in Montreal, 1628–1986 (1989); The Road to Now (1997)

representative_people.name: Barry Cahill
representative_people.context: A Nova Scotia archivist who calls the Black Loyalist interpretation a scholars' myth that sidelines the enslaved; Walker replies in the same issue.
representative_people.works: "The Black Loyalist Myth in Atlantic Canada" (1999)

representative_people.name: Afua Cooper
representative_people.context: Historian and poet; co-author of We're Rooted Here (1994) and author of a history of slavery in New France through the trial of Marie-Joseph Angélique (2006, extension).
representative_people.works: co-author, We're Rooted Here (1994); The Hanging of Angélique (2006)

representative_people.name: Harvey Amani Whitfield
representative_people.context: Studies the Black Refugees of the War of 1812 and Loyalist slavery in the Maritimes, against the narrative of Canada as a land of freedom (extension).
representative_people.works: Blacks on the Border (2006); North to Bondage (2016)

representative_people.name: Sarah-Jane Mathieu
representative_people.context: Connects Black migration, sleeping car porters and their union, and segregation in Canada with Black diaspora history (extension).

representative_people.name: Barrington Walker
representative_people.context: Studies how blackness was articulated in Ontario's criminal courts (extension).

representative_people.name: David Austin
representative_people.context: Studies Black Power, Caribbean radicals and state security in sixties Montreal (extension).
representative_people.works: "All Roads Led to Montreal" (2007); Fear of a Black Nation (2013)

strands.title: Slavery in New France and British North America
strands.focus: From Trudel's francophone history (1960) and dictionary (1990) of slavery in French Canada to Cahill's 1999 call to 'reclaim the history of the slaves' and post-2000 studies of enslaved people in Montreal and the Maritimes (Cooper, Mackey, Whitfield), which reviewers read as correcting the image of Canada as a haven.
strands.works: Trudel (1960, 1990, 2004); Cahill (1999); Gay (2004); Cooper (2006); Mackey (2010; French 2013); Whitfield (2016)

strands.title: Black Loyalists, refugees and the settlements of Canada West
strands.focus: Winks's survey (1971) and Walker's Black Loyalists (1976), with Walker's study guide (1980) and Hill's introductory history (1981); Silverman's Canada West (1985) as Walker's example of the 'Victims' orientation; the Black Refugees of 1812 (Whitfield 2006).

strands.title: Work, migration and discrimination
strands.focus: Discrimination in work, war, migration and law: Walker's CHA publication (1985) and study of First World War recruitment (1989), Calliste on porters (1987) and Caribbean labour migration (1993–94), Shepard on Black Oklahomans 'deemed unsuitable' (1997), Ruck's community history of the Black Battalion (1987); after 2000, Mathieu on porters and the colour line and Barrington Walker on the courts (2010).
strands.works: Walker (1985, 1989); Calliste (1987, 1993–94); Ruck (1987, community history); Shepard (1997); Mathieu (2010); B. Walker (2010)

strands.title: Community, women and oral history
strands.focus: Black women's history through interviews and collective scholarship: Brand's narratives of working women (1991), the six-author We're Rooted Here (1994), Williams's Black Montreal (1989, 1997); Flynn on Black and Caribbean nurses after 2000. Walker in 1997 noted that Black women were receiving increasing attention. The six coauthors of We're Rooted Here (1994) are Bristow, Brand, Carty, Cooper, Hamilton and Shadd; shared methods or positions are not inferred.
strands.works: Williams (1989, 1997); Brand (1991); Bristow et al. (1994); Flynn (2011)

strands.title: Africville: from social problem to community
strands.focus: Walker reads the Africville literature as an allegory of the field: Clairmont and Magill's relocation study (1971; 1974; 1987) moves toward victimization while its wording shifts from 'enclave' to 'community', and the Africville Genealogical Society's Spirit of Africville (1992) gives the community perspective; Nelson (2008) later reads the razing as a geography of racism.

strands.title: Orientations, myth and revision
strands.focus: The field's self-reflection: Walker's critical review of Winks (1971, cited in Walker 1999); Walker's five orientations (1997), with Landon and Riddell as 'Clients', Silverman as 'Victims', Stouffer (1992) giving 'Clients' new credibility and Brand's introduction as 'Survivors'; Cahill's 'Black Loyalist Myth' and Walker's reply (Acadiensis 1999); a regional bibliography (Morton and Wright 2021, extension).
strands.works: Stouffer (1992); Walker (1997, 1999); Cahill (1999); Morton and Wright (2021)

strands.title: Black Montreal and Quebec
strands.focus: A Quebec literature in both languages: Trudel's francophone slavery studies, Williams on Black Montreal (1989, 1997), a contemporary participants' collection on the 1969 Sir George Williams affair (Forsythe 1971, not scholarship), and after 2000 Gay (2004), Austin on Black Power and security (2007, 2013), Mackey (2010; French 2013) and Mills on Haiti and Quebec (2016). Of 177 PhDs citing the field, 16 are at francophone universities; Mackey's readers are mostly francophone (5 of 9).
strands.works: Trudel (1960); Forsythe, ed. (1971); Williams (1989, 1997); Gay (2004); Austin (2007, 2013); Mackey (2010); Mills (2016)

extension_coverage.note: Post-2000 works are selected extension milestones chosen by PhD citation counts, not a reviewed post-2000 field. Uncovered here: Black Canadian geography and cultural studies (McKittrick, Walcott), Black education history (Aladejebi), Maynard's Policing Black Lives (2017).

uptake.definition: Strict History PhDs completed 2009–2026 (n=1303) citing at least one of 494 curated Black Canadian history work records (titles and authors reviewed by hand in the citation graph; includes some older and primary-source accounts on Black Canada). Counted by dissertation, not citation. Details in evidence.json.

q46_reproduction.note: The Q46 title regex reproduces exactly (104 PhDs, 5.6% → 8.9%), but 25 of the 104 reach the set only through non-Canadian works matched by 'esclavage' (slavery in France, medieval Europe, the Antilles) or 'race and recruitment' (the Indian Army); it also misses most of the field (Mathieu, Barrington Walker, Williams, Calliste, Brand, Africville). The curated count is 177.

dissertations_on_black_canadian_subjects.note: By reading titles and bibliographies, 11 dissertations (2013–2025) are on Black Canadian subjects and one more in part. The Q46 figure of 23 came from a title regex ('black', 'slaver', 'esclav', 'noir') that also matched Natal, Chicago, the Black Sea, black bears, Florentine and Louisianan slavery and Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag; only 6 of those 23 are on Black Canadian subjects. Supervisors include James Walker (2), Barrington Walker (2) and Stephanie Bangarth (2).

uptake.caveat: Laval is undercounted in the corpus (download in progress). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; engagement lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Walker's 1997 essay (full text read) identifies five orientations in African-Canadian historiography by the role assigned to Black people, ties the Community turn to Black Power, Black pride and social history, and to 'the collective nature of the black struggle in North America'. Later Canadian work is published in and framed by Black diaspora history: Mathieu (abstract) connects Black migrants and porters to 'black diaspora history during the Jim Crow era'; Austin publishes in the Journal of African American History (2007, metadata). Moved here from cdn_immigration_ethnicity (cie_rel_02). The atlas entry's own scope note warns that diaspora links do not make Black histories one national tradition: this is a contribution, not a sub-field.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Black migration and racialized immigration control
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Calliste (abstract read) shows immigration officials restricting Black Caribbean settlers while employers recruited their labour, 1900–32; Shepard (via Walker 1997) studies African American migration from Oklahoma to the prairies before 1914 and, by its subtitle, the racism the migrants met; Mathieu (abstract) joins immigration and Black diaspora history. Black Canadian history is not a sub-field of immigration history: of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works, 45% engage cdn_immigration_ethnicity (lift 3.4; 39% and lift 3.0 on the Q46 definition). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

Austin's Fear of a Black Nation (description read) centres the 1968 Congress of Black Writers and the Black-led protest at Sir George Williams University; Forsythe's 1971 collection is a contemporary participants' account, not scholarship; Austin 2007 is title-level. All selected scholarship is post-2000, so this is an extension comparison; cdn_sixties declined a black – cdn_sixties edge for the same reason, and this edge is the narrower Canadian pair. PhD context: 40% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage cdn_sixties (lift 2.8).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Slavery in New France and Black Quebec
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Trudel, a Laval historian of New France on the Quebec roster, wrote the francophone history of slavery in French Canada (1960, checked against Hamelin's RHAF review heading) and its dictionary (1990, which Walker 1997 lists among works on slavery); Gay (2004) and the French edition of Mackey (2013) continue a francophone strand, and Mackey is read mostly at francophone universities (5 of 9 PhDs). Bibliographic level only; no checked text frames the two literatures against each other. PhD context: 16 of 177 PhDs citing Black Canadian history works are at francophone universities; 37% engage quebec_historiography (lift 2.3).

Walker (1997, full text) notes that 'black women have been receiving increasing attention' and uses Brand's No Burden to Carry as his example of the Survivors orientation; We're Rooted Here (1994) is a six-author volume of African Canadian women's history; Bonner's review (read) calls Flynn's Moving Beyond Borders a contribution to 'a sparse literature relative to the lives of African Canadian women'. PhD context: 61% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage cdn_women_gender (lift 2.4).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Black workers, porters and segmented labour
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Calliste (1987, title-level) treats Black sleeping car porters as an 'ethnically submerged split labour market'; Mathieu (abstract read) follows porters and their union, white railwaymen's demands for a segregated workforce, and porters as civil-rights leaders. PhD context: 48% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage cdn_working_class (lift 2.2). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Black soldiers and race in recruitment
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Walker's 'Race and Recruitment in World War I' (CHR 1989, metadata) is the scholarly study of visible-minority enlistment in the CEF that cdn_military also uses, and Ruck's Black Battalion (1987) is a community history of the No. 2 Construction Battalion; Walker 1997 lists both in his reading for African-Canadian history. Title-level only. PhD context: 17% of PhDs citing Black Canadian history works engage cdn_military (lift 1.2), so this is a narrow shared subject, not a shared readership.

relationships_considered_not_proposed.reason: No checked source frames Black Canadian history through settler colonialism (Maynard 2017 and McKittrick are unreviewed; Rushforth 2012 concerns Indigenous slavery). PhD lift 2.5 (28% share) is not evidence of a framing.
Omi and Winant are not cited in the checked texts; Walker 1997 classifies by orientation, not by racial formation.
Backhouse's Colour-Coded (1999) and her Viola Desmond article are in Walker's 1997 reading list but were not checked for this draft.
No checked source; Indigenous slavery (panis) is outside this selection.
Declined in drafts/cdn_sixties; this draft proposes the narrower cdn_black_history – cdn_sixties comparison instead (cbh_rel_03).

question_resolutions.summary: New entry created on the user's decision of 2026-10-12. The Black Canadian strand, four sources (cdnsrc_trudel_1960, cdnsrc_winks_1971, cdnsrc_walker_1976, cdnsrc_walker_1997a, same ids) and the contribution edge to black (now cbh_rel_01) moved here from cdn_immigration_ethnicity. Uptake recomputed: the Q46 regex gives 104 PhDs but includes non-Canadian slavery works; a hand-curated set gives 177 (9.5% → 15.3%). Of the 23 'Black' dissertation titles, 6 are Black Canadian subjects; 11 dissertations in all (one more in part).
